narrative_statement: When learners differ by diagnostic expertise level, diagnostic reasoning instruction provides instructional input that can shape relative reliance on analytic and similarity-based processes, leading to processing reliance that is modifiable by instruction and dependent on expertise.

When learners are novice diagnosticians, diagnostic reasoning instruction provides feature-oriented and similarity-trusting instructions, triggering a feature-oriented and similarity-trusting cognitive orientation, leading to improved performance.

When newly trained ECG novices receive no explicit reasoning guidance, an interfering feature prompt may induce greater analytic-tendency reliance, leading to lower accuracy in the no-instruction condition.

When novice diagnosticians receive no explicit reasoning guidance, an incorrect diagnostic suggestion may induce greater non-analytic tendency reliance, leading to lower accuracy under incorrect than correct suggestions.

When novice diagnosticians learn ECG diagnosis, feature-oriented and similarity-trusting instructions cue avoidance of single-mode reasoning, leading to improved diagnostic accuracy compared with unguided intuitions.

When novice diagnosticians face misleading feature or diagnosis suggestions, combined reasoning instructions cue them to trust familiarity while checking features, leading to no decline in performance under misleading information.

When newly trained ECG novices receive explicit diagnostic reasoning instruction, feature-oriented and similarity-trusting instructions plus list support trigger guided combined strategy use, leading to higher diagnostic accuracy than spontaneous reasoning.

When newly trained ECG novices encounter ECGs previously seen during training, practice with ECG examples triggers similarity-based processes, leading to higher and retained accuracy for previously seen ECGs.

When newly trained ECG novices are left to spontaneous reasoning, natural-strategy instructions with optional feature-list use trigger unguided or less effective strategy implementation, leading to lower accuracy than explicit combined reasoning instruction.

When ECG categories share features and are easily confusable, contrastive learning provides compare-and-contrast prompts that trigger diagnosticity awareness and reduced premature closure, leading to greater diagnostic accuracy than non-contrastive learning.

When learners face complex diagnostic tasks, erroneous worked examples combined with elaborated explanatory feedback provide severe errors and explanations, triggering error identification and comparison with correct solutions, leading to the highest diagnostic knowledge scores.

When learners work in complex diagnostic learning environments, erroneous examples paired with right-or-wrong KCR feedback provide errors without explanation, failing to induce deep conceptual understanding and leaving learners vulnerable to superficial processing, leading to poor diagnostic knowledge performance.

When worked examples are studied under realistic unrestricted time conditions, elaborated feedback provides additional explanations, triggering processing of feedback information, leading to longer learning time, although time-on-task itself was not associated with diagnostic knowledge.

When students have a deficient diagnostic knowledge base, computer-supported case-based worked examples provide diagnostic worked cases and a structured process schema, triggering lower cognitive load and investment in schema construction, leading to an effective approach and sustained conceptual knowledge gains.

When year 2 medical students participate in a course designed to promote clinical reasoning, the clinical reasoning-oriented course exposure is associated with increased confidence in diagnostic reasoning, leading alongside a significant gain in clinical reasoning on a script concordance test.

When medical students have a correct initial diagnosis, querying the initial diagnostic hypothesis provides an initial hypothesis query prompt that appears to trigger thinking during the query, with no harm to the correct diagnosis.

When medical students have an incorrect initial diagnosis, querying the initial diagnostic hypothesis provides an initial hypothesis query prompt that appears to trigger thinking during the query, leading to rectification of the incorrect diagnosis and reduced diagnostic error.

When learners have low initial attraction to laboratory careers, clinical pathology courses or instructors and exposure to laboratory data revealing hidden disease can trigger discovery of laboratory data’s explanatory power, leading to piqued interest in clinical pathology.

When diagnosticians have expertise developed over years of diligent study and practice and face a cascade of data abnormalities, diligent study and practice is described as supporting logical connection to disease mechanisms, leading to identification of failing organ systems.

When students are in clinical reasoning seminars, a case-based seminar with an explicit cognitive-features focus is designed to bring insight into cognitive features of their reasoning, and the intervention is reported to improve aspects of diagnostic competence.

When undergraduate primary care rotations are short, video-enriched virtual patient cases provide multiplied verbal and non-verbal patient encounters, triggering students to practise and refine GP reasoning, leading to accelerated acquisition of targeted clinical reasoning skills.

When primary care reasoning involves restricted rule-outs and probabilistic reasoning, diagnostic decision tree VP cases provide virtual experience of real-time reasoning techniques, triggering estimation and adjustment of diagnostic probability, leading to intended acquisition of primary-care-specific clinical reasoning skills.

When GP diagnostic approaches are not explicitly taught to medical students, video-enriched virtual patient cases provide virtual prior experience with real patient videos, triggering stimulated clinical diagnostic reasoning, leading to primary-care-specific clinical reasoning skill acquisition.

When short student rotations limit follow-up of and reflection on patients, time-compressed virtual patient cases provide compressed longitudinal disease and treatment effects, triggering observation of test-of-time and treatment strategies, leading to learning and construction of clinical reasoning skills.

When students are on a six-week primary care rotation, self-directed video VP cases provide real patient video recordings, triggering appreciation of real-patient VP videos, leading to perceived usefulness for developing consulting skills.

When students have limited familiarity with a clinical topic, a prompt to read cases and generate self-explanations without feedback triggers active sense-making and causal linking, leading to better subsequent diagnostic performance.

When learners’ illness scripts are less developed for an unfamiliar clinical area, minimal self-explanation instructions without feedback trigger inference generation and integration with prior knowledge, leading to better diagnostic performance one week later.

When students already have well-defined illness scripts for familiar problems, the self-explanation case prompt leaves limited room for elaboration and reconstruction, leading to no diagnostic-performance benefit.

When students use evPaeds, it provides individual or small-group opportunities to practise clinical reasoning, associated with student engagement in clinical reasoning practice and with student popularity and positive reception.

When students have had limited meaningful exposure to decision-making responsibility during FY1 shadowing, complex individual decision-making situations in simulation trigger recognition of inadequate information gathering and improved understanding of personal responsibility, leading to more objective prioritisation learning and greater preparedness for FY1 work.

When students have no prior prioritisation training and are unfamiliar with pagers, multiple tasks and acutely unwell patients trigger stress and overload, leading to loss of focus and incomplete structured assessment.

When final-year students near transition to junior doctor receive a tutorial focused on clinical decision-making theory, the provided theoretical understanding can trigger perceived lack of relevance and limited perceived benefit, leading to no discernable difference in described approaches to decision making.

When students are familiar with existing structured tools, a readily available SBAR structure beside the phones triggers greater comfort and reduced fear during senior referral, leading to uptake of SBAR in the simulator session.
When students have not previously used AM I HERO NOW, the mnemonic decision-making tool triggers perceptions of excessive time demand and complexity, leading to non-use during simulated practice.

When students lack well-developed illness scripts, structured reflection provides a detailed multi-diagnosis reflection procedure that may trigger high cognitive load, exhaustion or initial confusion, leading to worse immediate-test performance than immediate or differential diagnosis conditions.

When students lack well-developed illness scripts, a speeded single-diagnosis task provides a reflection-minimising procedure, triggering simply giving a diagnosis, leading to less effective learning than structured reflection.

When teaching commonly asks students to generate alternative hypotheses, differential diagnosis practice provides an alternative-diagnoses prompt, triggering only partial reflection and limited contradictory- and absent-finding checking, leading to less learning than structured reflection.

When students are not yet likely to have well-developed illness scripts, structured reflection provides prompts to identify supporting and opposing findings, triggering elaboration and knowledge reorganisation, leading to superior delayed diagnosis of new exemplars compared with other conditions.

When students lack well-developed illness scripts, structured reflection provides step-by-step matching of case findings to alternative diagnoses, triggering proposed enrichment of stored illness scripts, leading to delayed-test learning relative to learning-phase performance.

When novice medical students receive the same factual information organised differently as a schema, the resource selectively modifies knowledge organisation into structured knowledge, but this leads to no improvement on factual knowledge questions.

When novice medical students practise simulated cardiac cases using an assigned schema framework, the resource triggers increased use of schema-based reasoning, leading to greater diagnostic accuracy for taught lesions.

When novice medical students with basic cardiac exam exposure receive a diagnostic schema framework grouped by clinical features, it triggers knowledge organisation into structured knowledge, leading to improved retained structured knowledge.

When learners encounter lesions included on the framework but not practised in the learning phase, a diagnostic schema framework grouped by clinical features triggers attention to schema-based distinguishing features, leading to greater diagnostic accuracy for untaught lesions.

When students face an unknown systolic murmur requiring integration of many findings, diagnosis-specific tables of clinical features can trigger identification of more incorrect features, which may derail reasoning and is associated with lower practical diagnostic accuracy than schema-based instruction.

When advanced students have prior endocrinology training, varied same-process clinical cases with official diagnosis feedback trigger reminders of previous cases and comparisons with prior knowledge, leading to learning about enabling conditions and consequences.

When students have incomplete and error-prone knowledge, a case-explanation format that supports reflection can trigger active biomedical debugging attempts, leading to partial remediation for some but ignored errors for others.

When students with prior clinical case exposure reason through varied same-process cases, the cases trigger faster and more secure case representations, contributing to implicit learning and stronger links between concepts.

When students have very poor or incomplete error-prone prior knowledge, unsupported similar-case reasoning with only reduced feedback leaves some unaware of errors or unable to solve them, so pathophysiology knowledge may not improve and biomedical integration remains insufficient.

When students are at the transition to clinical practice, asking them to diagnose, explain and learn from cases without a suggested learning strategy can leave many showing no explicit learning processes, leading to no observed learning for half of the group.

When novice diagnosticians diagnose standardized-patient cases, structured reflection diagnostic case practice provides a differential diagnosis evidence table, triggering consideration of alternatives and conflicting findings, leading to improved diagnostic accuracy.

When cases are too complex relative to students’ medical knowledge, the differential diagnosis evidence table may still trigger consideration of alternatives and conflicting findings, but that reasoning may not be helpful, limiting diagnostic benefit.

When the clinical presentation is typical, routine usual diagnostic reasoning with a simple answer sheet can enable heuristic pattern recognition, leading to few diagnostic errors and constraining additional benefit from the analytic reasoning table.

When cases are less familiar because students have had less prior exposure, self-explanation diagnostic case solving provides opportunities to link biomedical and clinical knowledge, triggering more active thinking and more biomedical inferences, leading to more coherent disease representations and better diagnosis of unfamiliar cases.

When clinical cases are already familiar, self-explanation diagnostic case solving still provides an opportunity to generate explanations, but it is associated with less biomedical inference activation and similar overall inference generation, corresponding with no demonstrated diagnostic benefit for familiar cases.

When learners have incomplete or error-prone prior knowledge, generating explanations to oneself triggers awareness of knowledge limits and attempts to detect and resolve misunderstandings, leading to knowledge restructuring and a more integrated representation.

When students’ specific knowledge is less elaborate, case text with clinical details used during self-explanation triggers students to stay closer to the text while actively constructing knowledge, leading to more paraphrasing and more errors.

When novice cytopathology learners are asked in the final test to combine analytic and nonanalytic strategies, the combined analytic-nonanalytic strategy instruction may trigger confusion, leading to reduced final-test discrimination and the accuracy-superiority hypothesis not being supported.

When naive observers work without expert assistance, minimal exposure to cytopathology images triggers self-generated helpful abnormal-cell features, leading to criteria resembling standard cytopathology features.

When novice cytopathology learners receive nonanalytic cytopathology image training, nonannotated normal-abnormal image pairs trigger a similarity-based first impression, leading to improved diagnostic performance and faster responses.

When novice cytopathology learners use analytic cytopathology feature training, a typed feature list with terminology explanation triggers sole feature-based analysis, leading to slower responses and no diagnostic accuracy advantage over nonanalytic training.

When novice cytopathology learners receive analytic cytopathology feature training, a typed feature list with terminology explanation triggers feature-based diagnostic analysis, leading to improved discrimination and fewer miss errors.

When non-expert surgical learners practise with repeated time-limited cases and solution-focused feedback, the game triggers testing and readjusting hypotheses, leading to improved performance in a second gaming session.

When surgical learners have prior video-game experience, a time-pressured competitive quiz-game format triggers enjoyment and challenge, leading to willingness to recommend the game and play voluntarily.
When student learners have limited clinical experience, a ten-second case time limit can trigger frustration, leading authors to conclude that the level of difficulty was too high for some students.

When learners have clinically different expertise levels, simulated biliary clinical cases trigger a perception that clinical experience is helpful, while expertise level enables higher case-solving accuracy among surgeons than less experienced groups.

When cases include non-textbook diagnostic courses, Casebook can provide organised records with error discussions, triggering students to examine causes and the course of error, leading to learning about consequences of diagnostic error.

When students have limited ward exposure, Casebook provides pools of EHR-based patient cases, triggering pattern recognition from multiple-case experience, leading to illness-script development for diagnosis.

When students need longitudinal observation of patient decision-making, Casebook provides temporally organised annotated records, triggering them to follow illness course and witness management effects, leading to learning clinical diagnostic reasoning and decision-making skills.

When undergraduate students are preparing for prototypical presentations they may encounter in first jobs, Casebook provides physician reasoning annotations, triggering understanding of physician thought processes, leading to decision-making skill learning from real cases.
When novices are not using nonanalytic reasoning, CFS training may provide an additional circumspection demand that may overwhelm cognitive load, leading to no observed reduction in diagnostic error.

When novice senior medical students worked through search-satisficing cases with two diagnoses, the CFS case-based seminar provided bias self-monitoring instruction and clinical case practice with feedback, triggering second-diagnosis search in some students, but leading to no significant second-diagnosis improvement over control.

When novice senior medical students faced availability-bias cases where a common diagnosis was plausible but incorrect, the CFS seminar provided search and availability bias explanation; nevertheless, common incorrect diagnosis selection remained frequent, leading to limited uncommon-diagnosis recognition with no difference between groups.

When cases had no correct second diagnosis, the CFS seminar provided search-satisficing bias instruction; students nevertheless oversearched for nonexistent second diagnoses, leading to incorrect second diagnoses without significant group differences.

When novice observers listen to expert reasoning, expert self-explanation example observation provides fast, non-analytic, abstract reasoning that can trigger difficulty relating the reasoning to their own knowledge, leading to expert models being no more effective than peer models.

When learners observe same-level peer models, peer self-explanation example observation provides examples containing irrelevant details and uncorrected errors, triggering little learning from such same-level examples and contributing to only subtle added value of SE models.

When jaundice is a rather unfamiliar topic for clerks, self-explanation diagnostic case solving provides written clinical cases that trigger knowledge elaboration and representation revision, leading to improved diagnostic accuracy and diagnostic performance on training cases.

When clinical reasoning is a complex less-structured skill, combining students’ own self-explanation with peer or expert audio models provides explicit examples and presumed immediate feedback that trigger extension and critical revision of knowledge representations, leading to immediate diagnostic accuracy improvement maintained after 1 week.

When example observation lacks active-processing prompts, natural SE example observation after students’ own SE provides raw clinical reasoning examples that may trigger passive listening, constraining the added value of SE models, including lack of added value on transfer cases.

When clerks face unfamiliar jaundice cases, self-explanation diagnostic case solving provides opportunities to generate explanations to oneself, triggering knowledge elaboration, monitoring and biomedical reactivation, leading to improved near-transfer diagnostic accuracy and performance.

When far-transfer diagnostic cases are difficult, resident SE examples without prompts provide silent sequences but no specific processing instructions, which may fail to elicit the critical active processing and additional self-explanation needed for transfer, leading to no clear far-transfer advantage over control.

When residents’ reasoning is cognitively congruent with clerks’ own, listening to elaborated resident self-explanations triggers easy comparison, elaboration and confirmation of ideas, leading to immediate improvement maintained over time.

When far-transfer diagnostic cases are difficult, resident SE examples with embedded prompts trigger additional self-explanation during listening and reactivation of pathophysiological mechanisms, leading to higher far-transfer accuracy and performance than control and higher performance than unprompted examples.

When students receive identical case content without key feature prompts, repeated case-based learning alone provides background information without highlighting tested aspects, triggering shorter engagement with study-only cases, leading to lower study-only item performance than tested items.

When students may lack exposure to relevant clinical problems in existing teaching, computer-assisted key feature testing provides standardised content and otherwise unavailable reasoning opportunities, triggering access to problem-solving knowledge, leading to enhanced procedural knowledge retention.

When students repeatedly encounter the same intervention items, key feature testing provides explanations of correct and incorrect options, triggering learning after failed retrieval, leading to subsequent correct answers on repeated items.

When Year 4 undergraduate medical students are learning clinical reasoning, repeated key feature test-enhanced case learning provides embedded key feature prompts and immediate feedback, triggering storage and retrieval of knowledge, leading to higher long-term retention scores.

When clinicians’ automated reasoning can risk missing critical information, teaching clinical reasoning provides an opportunity to review their own reasoning pathways, triggering reflection on and improvement of reasoning, leading to proposed potential practice benefits.

When students are already familiar with how the clinician reasons through a consultation, the student performance consultation provides teacher interjections with reasoning questions when reasoning is unclear, triggering the student’s reasoning to stay on track, leading to guided performance of consultation reasoning steps.

When novice diagnosticians with limited clinical experience are expected to pick up clinical reasoning tacitly, automated unarticulated clinician reasoning triggers difficulty grasping expert reasoning, leading to a barrier to learning.

When students find applying knowledge to patient care complex and challenging, a comprehension-stage teacher-led consultation provides hypothesis-listing pauses and reasoning-probe questions, triggering active tracking of demonstrated reasoning, leading to the student determining primary and differential hypotheses during the consultation.

When novice diagnosticians have limited clinical experience, a three-consultation clinical reasoning skill framework provides explicit modelling and explanation of expert reasoning, triggering understanding of expert thinking and reasoning, leading to theorised development of clinical reasoning ability.
